title: openssl.cnf
summary: Find the configuration file openssl reads, read its sections, and pick the extensions a certificate gets.

text: Every openssl command reads a configuration file, openssl.cnf, in the folder openssl version -d prints. Its defaults decide what you get when you don't say.
- OPENSSL_CONF=FILE points openssl at another file; -config FILE does it for one req or ca command.
- On Rocky, the file includes the system's crypto policy: update-crypto-policies --set changes what the programs that follow it accept (OpenSSL, GnuTLS, NSS, Java…).
The file is made of sections: a [ name ], then one name = value per line, and # starts a comment. Each command reads its own section, which can name others.
- -extensions NAME picks the section of extensions the certificate gets; -extfile FILE reads it from another file.
$ openssl x509 -req -in mid.csr -CA root.pem -CAkey root.key -CAcreateserial -extfile lab.cnf -extensions v3_intermediate -out mid.pem
openssl ca turns a folder into a small CA: it signs requests and records each certificate it signed in index.txt. Its section says where everything is.
- serial and crlnumber hold the next numbers, in hex.
- copy_extensions = copy takes the SAN from the request, but keeps the section's own basicConstraints: set it there. copyall lets the request win, CA:TRUE included.
